# ISO 26262 and 21488

## 1. ISO 26262 (Functional Safety, FuSa)

| Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Focus                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Goal:** To prevent unreasonable risk due to **malfunction** of electrical and/or electronic (E/E) systems.                                                                                                                                                          | **Process Rigor & Defect Prevention.** It governs the entire product development lifecycle (the V-Model), ensuring design correctness and reliability. |
| **Core Concept:** **ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level).** Determined by HARA (Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment), ASIL (A-D) defines the required rigor for development, testing, and documentation to manage risk proportional to the severity of a failure. | **Key Output:** Verification Reports proving component traceability, code coverage (MC/DC), and diagnostic coverage against hardware faults.           |

<img title="" src="file:///Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2026-01-05-10-00-19-image.png" alt="" width="590">

## 2. ISO 21448 (Safety of the Intended Functionality, SOTIF)

<img title="" src="file:///Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2026-01-05-10-00-35-image.png" alt="" width="593">

| Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Focus                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Goal:** To prevent unreasonable risk due to **functional insufficiency** or performance limitations of the system, *even when the hardware and software are operating correctly.*                                  | **Performance Adequacy & Scenario Management.** It focuses on defining the ODD (Operational Design Domain) and identifying hazardous scenarios caused by sensor limitations, lack of knowledge, or confusing external environments. |
| **Core Concept:** **Triggering Condition.** SOTIF requires mitigating risks arising from known performance limitations and demonstrating acceptable residual risk for scenarios that fall outside the validated ODD. | **Key Output:** Requirements for the **Checker Stack** (e.g., OOD detection) and statistical validation of safety margins within the ODD.                                                                                           |

---

## 3. Statistical Methods for Safety Claim Validation

The following table summarizes the types of statistical analysis used to provide the quantitative evidence required by these standards in the context of an ADS.

| Statistical Method                                    | Primary Safety Claim Supported                                                                                                                                  | Supporting Standard                           | Example Application in ADS                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Proportion (Z-Test) & Poisson Confidence Interval** | **Failure Rate Reduction & Upper Bound Risk.** To state, with high confidence, that the true failure rate is below a mandated safety target (λUB​<λtarget​).    | ISO 26262 (Validation of residual risk)       | Quantifying the **ASIL D Trigger Rate** (critical failures per million hours) and proving improvement over a baseline system.     |
| **Code/Branch Coverage Metrics (MC/DC)**              | **Completeness of Code Verification.** To prove that the checker software has been tested against nearly all possible input logic paths.                        | ISO 26262 (Unit and Integration Verification) | Proving the deterministic **ASIL Checker Stack** adheres to 100% MC/DC required by the standard for high-ASIL components.         |
| **Extreme Value Analysis (EVA: GEV/GPD)**             | **Robustness against Catastrophic, Unobserved Events.** To predict and quantify the probability of the worst-case scenario (the long tail of the distribution). | ISO 21448 (SOTIF Residual Risk)               | Predicting the **Return Level**—the minimum TTC value expected over 10 million miles—to ensure adequate safety margin.            |
| **Bootstrapping**                                     | **Confidence in Complex/Non-Parametric Metrics.** To empirically derive reliable Confidence Intervals for mathematically opaque safety metrics.                 | ISO 21448 (SOTIF Validation)                  | Calculating the confidence bounds for a custom, non-linear metric like **Time-Integrated Safety Debt** or an ML confidence score. |
| **ROC/Recall Analysis (Checker Specific)**            | **Efficacy of Fault Detection.** To quantify the sensitivity of the safety checker in detecting true functional failures by the primary ML system.              | ISO 26262 / SOTIF (Verification)              | Proving the **Independent Obstacle Clearance Checker** maintains a 99.99% Recall rate during systematic fault injection testing.  |

# ASIL lifecycle

The ASIL development lifecycle is not merely a set of testing steps; it is a **prescriptive, rigorous process** that governs every phase of development, development, and retirement for an E/E system, ensuring safety is built-in from the start.

This lifecycle is formally defined by the **ISO 26262 standard (Parts 3 through 8)** and is structured around the **V-Model**. The V-Model ensures that every requirement defined on the left side (definition) is verified and validated on the right side (testing).

## The ASIL Development Lifecycle (The V-Model)

### 1. The Left Arm: Specification and Design (Requirements Down)

This phase defines *what* the system must do and *how* it must be safe. The required rigor is determined by the ASIL level (ASIL A < ASIL D).

| Phase                                             | Goal                                                                                                              | ASIL-D Specific Requirement                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **A. Item Definition & HARA (Part 3)**            | Define the item (system scope) and use the HARA to determine the ASIL for all safety-critical functions.          | **Formal HARA Documentation:** Traceability from every potential malfunction to its ASIL requirement (e.g., "Loss of braking (S3/E3/C3) requires ASIL D").                                  |
| **B. Safety Requirements Specification (Part 3)** | Derive technical Safety Requirements (TSRs) from the ASIL level.                                                  | **Completeness and Consistency:** Requirements must be unambiguous and verifiable. Specific methods are mandated for defining safety mechanisms (e.g., diagnostic coverage, reaction time). |
| **C. System Design (Part 4)**                     | Define the overall architecture, including hardware and software redundancy, and FFI (Freedom from Interference). | **Architectural Safety Analysis:** Detailed documentation proving the separation of ASIL components (e.g., ensuring the non-ASIL ML model cannot corrupt the ASIL-D checker's memory).      |
| **D. Software/Hardware Design (Part 6/5)**        | Detailed design and implementation specifications for individual components.                                      | **Software Tool Qualification:** All development tools (compilers, debuggers) must be qualified to ensure they introduce no systematic faults into the ASIL-D code.                         |

### 2. The Base: Implementation (Coding)

This phase is where the code is written, adhering strictly to the design specifications.

| Phase                                              | Goal                                        | ASIL-D Specific Requirement                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **E. Software/Hardware Implementation (Part 6/5)** | Writing the code and building the hardware. | **Coding Standards:** Strict enforcement of coding standards (e.g., MISRA C++). **Static Analysis:** Mandatory use of static analysis tools to verify adherence to safety rules *before* compilation. |

### 3. The Right Arm: Verification and Validation (Testing Up)

This phase ensures that the implemented system meets all safety requirements defined on the left arm. Rigor increases as you move up the V.

| Phase                                          | Goal                                                                                                           | ASIL-D Specific Requirement                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **F. Unit Verification (Part 6)**              | Testing individual software modules/functions (bottom of the right arm).                                       | **Coverage Mandates:** Requirement for 100% **MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage)**—proving that every Boolean condition within a decision affects the decision outcome. |
| **G. Software Integration & Testing (Part 6)** | Testing how integrated software components (e.g., sensor driver communicating with the checker) work together. | **Fault Injection Testing:** Required to prove the diagnostic coverage mechanisms (e.g., watchdogs) work correctly when hardware/software faults are artificially injected.       |
| **H. System Verification (Part 4)**            | Testing the fully integrated system against the TSRs (Technical Safety Requirements).                          | **Deterministic Testing:** Test reports must prove that the system can transition to a safe state (MRC) within the required time limits under defined fault conditions.           |
| **I. Safety Validation (Part 4)**              | Final test of the overall safety goals against the HARA results (top of the V).                                | **<mark>Statistical Proof</mark>:** Providing the quantitative evidence (e.g., λUB​ from Poisson analysis) that the residual risk meets the ASIL-D target.                        |

### 4. Safety Management and Supporting Processes (Parts 2, 7, 8)

Throughout the entire lifecycle, supporting activities ensure the integrity of the process:

| Process                        | Description                                                                                                                      | Relevance                                                              |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Safety Management (Part 2)** | Planning, defining roles (PESS team), defining quality records, and managing the overall safety plan.                            | Ensures accountability and traceability throughout the entire project. |
| **Configuration Management**   | Ensuring that every change to the software, hardware, or documentation is tracked, reviewed, and linked to verification results. | Essential for managing changes to ASIL-rated checker code.             |
| **Confirmation Measures**      | Independent reviews (often by third-party auditors) to confirm that the ASIL-D process was followed correctly.                   | Final sign-off required for certification.                             |

In summary, the ASIL development lifecycle transforms a risk score (ASIL D) into a mandate for **traceability, rigor, redundancy, and proof** at every stage, ensuring that safety is provably managed across the entire V-Model.

# Notes

- It’s important to look at rates of events (incidents per mile) instead of absolute counts. Waymo is growing its operations in the cities we operate in. With more driving miles come more absolute collisions. It’s critical to consider the total miles driven to accurately calculate incident rates. If you do not consider the miles driven, it may appear like incidents are increasing while in reality the rate of incidents could be going down.
- Confidence intervals for Incidents Per Million Miles (IPMM) crash rates were computed using a Poisson Exact method. The confidence intervals for the percent reduction used a Clopper-Pearson binomial described in Nelson (1970). Both confidence intervals were assessed at a 95% confidence level. These confidence intervals use the same methods as described in [Kusano et al.](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/15389588.2024.2380786) (2023). 

# Rave checklist

- Sensitivity analyses, in particular, can show the differences among diverse analytical strategies

- Consider outcome data transformations to help overcome limitations and address new research questions safety impact approach assign an injury risk-based value to each event using the dynamics of the crash and established injury risk curves

- Quantify uncertainty of the estimates with statistical testing or other methods: It is best practice to leverage statistical methods to quantify uncertainty in retrospective safety impact analyses. There are a wide variety of methods that can be used in this context, ranging from normal/Poisson confidence intervals to various regression models that account for covariates and other issues. Researchers should use appropriate statistical methods to report standard errors and/or confidence intervals for any descriptive statistics or crash rate comparisons presented. The use of statistical testing accompanied with thorough documentation about the appropriateness of using the particular test or distribution choice given the data (e.g., related to normality or other methodological constraints) is suggested. For uncertainty in elements for which distributions are not known, sensitivity analysis and bootstrapping approaches can be useful. It is also important to describe other sources of uncertainty that were not accounted for in the study and their potential effect on the results.

- Consider outcome data transformations to help overcome limitations and address new research questions

- Counts and proportions are commonly used for categorical variables. Measures of central tendency and variance are commonly used to describe continuous variables.

# Counfunding variables

Dealing with confounding variables involves [study design techniques](https://www.google.com/search?q=study+design+techniques&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgAEAM) like randomization, matching, and restriction to prevent them, and [statistical methods](https://www.google.com/search?q=statistical+methods&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgAEAQ) (stratification, regression) to adjust for them during analysis, with randomization being the most powerful but not always feasible, while good design is key to isolating true effects. 

During Study Design (Prevention)

- [Randomization](https://www.google.com/search?q=Randomization&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgAEAo): The best method, randomly assigning participants to groups (treatment/control) to evenly distribute known and unknown confounders, like in a randomized controlled trial (RCT).

- [Restriction](https://www.google.com/search?q=Restriction&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgAEAw): Limiting your study sample to a homogeneous group (e.g., only non-smokers) to remove variability from a confounder.

- [Matching](https://www.google.com/search?q=Matching&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgAEA4): Pairing subjects in different groups who are similar on key characteristics (age, gender, baseline health) to balance confounders.

- **[Control Groups](https://www.google.com/search?q=Control+Groups&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgBEAE):** Including a baseline group that doesn't get the intervention to compare against.

- [Blinding](https://www.google.com/search?q=Blinding&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgCEAE): (Single/Double-blind) Prevents participant or researcher expectations from biasing results, controlling for psychological confounders. 

During Data Analysis (Adjustment)

- [Stratification](https://www.google.com/search?q=Stratification&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgEEAE): Analyzing data within subgroups (strata) where the confounder is constant (e.g., analyzing results for each age group separately).
- [Multivariate Analysis](https://www.google.com/search?q=Multivariate+Analysis&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgEEAM) (e.g., Regression): Including confounders as variables in statistical models (like multiple regression) to estimate and adjust their influence on the outcome.
- **[Sensitivity Analysis](https://www.google.com/search?q=Sensitivity+Analysis&sca_esv=d499cf97fcbe8b52&sxsrf=AE3TifMWIvNdR48FCZ_YlO_NxS2m5tciUg%3A1765726817346&ei=Ydo-aY7uFOixur8Pib-38AU&oq=how+to+deal&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiC2hvdyB0byBkZWFsKgIIADILEAAYgAQYkQIYigUyCBAAGIAEGLEDMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgAQyBRAAGIAEMggQLhiABBixAzIIEAAYgAQYsQMyBRAAGIAEMgUQABiABDIFEAAYgARI9uEKUN0IWIYRcAN4AJABAJgBpgGgAboJqgEDMi45uAEByAEA-AEBmAIOoALsCcICBxAAGLADGB7CAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIOEC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYxwHCAg4QABiABBixAxiDARiKBcICDhAuGIAEGLEDGIMBGIoFwgIREC4YgAQYsQMY0QMYgwEYxwHCAgsQABiABBixAxiDAcICCxAuGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIKEAAYgAQYQxiKBZgDAIgGAZAGBpIHBDMuMTGgB5dssgcEMC4xMbgH5gnCBwYwLjExLjPIByGACAA&sclient=gws-wiz-serp&ved=2ahUKEwjvmJ3bt72RAxU6I0QIHReBBNQQgK4QegYIAAgEEAU):** Testing how robust your findings are by changing assumptions about potential confounders. 

Key Considerations

- **Identify first:** Understand potential confounders (variables related to both exposure and outcome) before starting.
- **Design is primary:** Good design minimizes confounders, but analysis can adjust for known ones.
- **Communicate:** Report potential confounders and their impact on findings.

# Retrospective Safety Impact Analysis

This paragraph outlines the statistical rigor necessary for **retrospective safety impact analysis**—the process of analyzing collected data (logs, shadow driving miles, or crash reports) to quantify the safety impact of an Automated Driving System (ADS).

The core message is that *all* reported safety metrics must come with quantified uncertainty (Confidence Intervals or Standard Errors).

Here is a thorough, detailed explanation of the methods mentioned, specifically in the context of ADS safety assurance.

## 1. Core Principle: Quantifying Uncertainty

In ADS safety assurance, **we are not interested in the *observed* failure rate (λ^), but rather the true failure rate (λ).** Since λ^ is just an estimate based on a finite amount of data, the **confidence interval (CI) provides the range where the true rate is likely to lie** (e.g., 99% sure the true rate is between A and B).

### Method A: Normal/Poisson Confidence Intervals

**These are used for quantifying the uncertainty around basic rates (the average frequency of events).**

#### Context: Normal Approximation (Used for means of continuous data)

- **When to Use:** Quantifying the uncertainty of a continuous safety metric's mean value, provided the sample size is large (e.g., the mean minimum TTC recorded during daily driving).
- **Safety Example:** You measure the mean **safe following distance** maintained by the ADS.
  - **Analysis:** Calculate the 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the mean using the formula: Mean±Zcritical​×(N​Standard Deviation​).
  - **Safety Assurance:** If the required safety margin for following distance is 50 meters, and your CI for the mean is [51.5m, 52.5m], you can confidently assure PESS that the system is meeting the margin *on average*.

#### Context: Poisson Confidence Intervals (Used for rates of rare, discrete events)

- **When to Use:** Quantifying the uncertainty around failure rates (λ) measured over long exposure units (N), such as TTC Floor violations per million miles. (As detailed in the previous section, the **Chi-Squared method** is typically used for exact Poisson CIs, especially for low k).
- **Safety Example:** Calculating the confidence in the **MRC Trigger Rate**.
  - **Analysis:** Use the Chi-Squared exact method to find the 99% CI for the true failure rate, given the observed k events in N miles.
  - **Safety Assurance:** This provides the critical **Upper Bound (λUB​)** for the failure rate, which is necessary to argue that the residual risk is below the ASIL target level (e.g., λUB​<10−7).

---

## 2. Advanced Regression Models

Simple confidence intervals ignore the complexity of the driving environment. Regression models allow researchers to control for external factors (covariates).

### Method B: Regression Models Accounting for Covariates

- **Goal:** To determine if a safety metric improvement is truly due to the new ADS feature, or just due to favorable driving conditions (less traffic, better weather).
- **Safety Example: Modeling Crash/Near-Miss Risk**
  - **Analysis:** Use a **Poisson Regression** or **Negative Binomial Regression** model (suitable for count data like crashes/triggers) where:
    - *Dependent Variable:* Count of critical events (k).
    - *Independent Variable of Interest:* System Type (Baseline vs. New ADS).
    - *Covariates:* Traffic density, time of day, road curvature, weather condition (wet/dry), and exposure unit (N, often incorporated as an offset in the model).
  - **Safety Assurance:** The model output provides an **Adjusted Rate Ratio (ARR)**. If the ARR is 0.5 (and statistically significant), it means the new system reduces the event rate by 50% *even after accounting for differences in traffic and weather between the test sets*. This is crucial for unbiased safety reporting.

---

## 3. Dealing with Unknown Distributions and Complex Data

In AV development, many metrics (especially those involving ML confidence scores or OOD scores) do not follow neat theoretical distributions.

### Method C: Sensitivity Analysis

- **Goal:** To assess how much the uncertainty in an input parameter affects the final safety conclusion.
- **Safety Example:** The uncertainty in the **Fusion Error Tolerance**.
  - **Analysis:** If your checker relies on an assumption (e.g., "radar sensor errors are normally distributed with $\sigma=0.1$m"), perform a sensitivity analysis by running your safety validation metrics assuming $\sigma=0.05$m and then $\sigma=0.2$m.
  - **Safety Assurance:** If the final λUB​ remains below the target threshold across a wide range of input uncertainties, the safety conclusion is deemed **robust**. If the conclusion fails quickly, it highlights a critical area for PESS to demand more verification data.

### Method D: Bootstrapping

- **Goal:** To empirically estimate the sampling distribution of a complex statistic when its theoretical distribution is unknown.
- **Safety Example:** Estimating the 99% CI for a **Time-Integrated Safety Debt Metric** (where the metric involves complex non-linear integration).
  - **Analysis:**
    1. Take B (e.g., B=1000) random samples with replacement from the original test data set (e.g., 1 million miles of driving logs).
    2. For each bootstrap sample, recalculate the safety debt metric.
    3. The resulting B metric values form an empirical distribution.
    4. Calculate the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of this distribution to get the 95% confidence interval for the metric.
  - **Safety Assurance:** Bootstrapping provides a non-parametric way to report robust confidence intervals for virtually any safety metric, regardless of how mathematically complex the metric calculation is, making it highly valuable for ML-driven metrics.

---

## 4. Documentation and Transparency (The Safety Case Requirement)

The final part of the requirement emphasizes accountability:

- **Documentation of Assumptions:** Every safety argument must explicitly state the assumptions made (e.g., "We used the Poisson model under the assumption that events are independent and rare, justified by observing an average rate of λ<10−4").
- **Unaccounted Uncertainty:** The safety case must describe known uncertainties that were *not* statistically modeled.
  - **Real Example:** "We did not account for inter-operator variability in the disengagement logs because the human driver reporting was not standardized. This introduces potential uncertainty in the Controllability(C) factor of the HARA." This demonstrates intellectual honesty, which is paramount in safety assurance.

Here is the revised summary table including a brief explanation of each method.

# Statistical Methods for ADS Safety Assurance: When to Use

| Method                                                  | Brief Explanation                                                                                                                                    | Type of Data / Goal                                                        | Safety Context / Application                                                                                                                                         | When to Use (Key Constraint)                                                                                                                           |
|:------------------------------------------------------- |:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |:-------------------------------------------------------------------------- |:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **1. Z-Test for Two Proportions**                       | Compares the probability of success/failure between two independent groups (Baseline vs. New System).                                                | Comparing two failure rates (Count data).                                  | Proving that a **New System** is statistically safer than a **Baseline System** by comparing critical event rates (e.g., TTC violation rates).                       | When you have two large populations (Baseline and New) and need to prove a **statistically significant reduction** in a rare event count.              |
| **2. Poisson Confidence Interval / Chi-Squared Method** | Calculates the confidence interval for the mean rate ($\lambda$) of discrete events occurring over time/space ($N$).                                 | Quantifying the uncertainty of a **rare event rate** ($\lambda$).          | Calculating the **Upper Bound ($\lambda_{UB}$)** of the true failure rate to demonstrate compliance with ASIL-defined risk targets (e.g., $10^{-7}$ failures/hour).  | When events are **rare and discrete** (count data $k$), and you need to state the worst-case risk guarantee given limited test exposure $N$.           |
| **3. Normal Approximation CI**                          | Uses the mean and standard error (SE) to set a range where the true mean is likely to fall.                                                          | Quantifying uncertainty of a **mean value** (Continuous data).             | Providing confidence intervals for average continuous safety margins, such as mean minimum following distance or average lateral lane offset.                        | When dealing with large sample sizes of **continuous, non-extreme** safety metrics whose distribution is roughly symmetric.                            |
| **4. Poisson / Negative Binomial Regression**           | Regression models used for predicting event counts, allowing control for external factors (covariates).                                              | Controlling for confounding variables in count data.                       | Determining the true safety impact of a new feature **after controlling for covariates** (traffic density, weather, road type).                                      | When comparing event rates across test sets that were driven under significantly **different environmental conditions**.                               |
| **5. Extreme Value Analysis (EVA: GEV/GPD)**            | A specialized set of models that mathematically describes the behavior of only the largest or smallest observed values (the data "tails").           | Modeling the distribution of **rare, high-severity events**.               | Predicting the **Return Level ($Z_T$)**—the worst-case TTC or G-force expected over the vehicle's lifetime (e.g., 100 million miles).                                | When extrapolating safety performance to levels of reliability ($>10^7$ miles) that cannot be observed in testing.                                     |
| **6. Bootstrapping**                                    | A non-parametric resampling technique that uses repeated sampling from the dataset to empirically estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic. | Quantifying uncertainty for **complex, non-parametric statistics**.        | Finding robust confidence intervals for metrics whose theoretical distribution is unknown (e.g., Time-Integrated Safety Debt, or confidence in a complex OOD score). | When the safety metric is mathematically complex or non-linear, making theoretical CI calculation impossible.                                          |
| **7. Sensitivity Analysis**                             | The process of changing input parameters/assumptions within a reasonable range to observe the effect on the final outcome.                           | Assessing the robustness of the final conclusion to **input assumptions**. | Testing how much uncertainty in sensor noise, fusion tolerance, or latency estimates affects the final computed risk bound ($\lambda_{UB}$).                         | When the final safety conclusion relies on **estimated parameters or tolerances** (e.g., noise $\sigma$) that carry their own measurement uncertainty. |

---

### Statistical Analysis for Extreme Reliability (Safety Case Extrapolation)

The goal is to answer the question: **"Given that we drove N miles and observed k critical failures, what is the 99% upper bound on the true failure rate (λ)?"**

### Step 1: Define the Safety Metric and Operational Unit

First, clearly define the safety event and the unit of exposure.

1. **Safety Event (E):** The critical failure event (e.g., TTC<1.0s, unauthorized high-speed lane departure, or successful activation of the safety checker).
2. **Exposure Unit (N):** The unit of operational time or distance (e.g., miles, hours, or specific maneuvers).

**Example:** We are validating the **MRC Trigger Rate** (critical failures that require the safety checker to activate) for a specific ODD (Highway driving, 60-75 mph).

### Step 2: Leverage Simulation and Data Synthesis

Since real-world test miles (Nreal​) are insufficient, the primary reliance is on extensive, high-fidelity simulation (Nsim​) and scenario testing.

1. **Simulation Testing:** Run millions of miles (Nsim​) in simulated environments, especially focusing on known-hazardous or high-risk scenarios identified by SOTIF analysis.
2. **Fidelity Validation:** Crucially, statistically validate the simulation environment itself. Compare the distribution of non-critical metrics (e.g., braking frequency, following distance distribution) between Nreal​ and Nsim​ using tests like the **Kolmogorov-Smirnov test**. This provides a **Conversion Factor (α)** for how much simulation mileage counts toward real-world assurance (e.g., 10 simulated miles ≈1 validated real mile).
3. **Data Synthesis:** Use scenario generation (e.g., fault injection) to deliberately force the critical failure event E to occur, which helps validate the **Recall** of the safety checker itself (see Example 3 in the previous response).

### Step 3: Statistical Bounding using the Poisson Distribution

The Poisson distribution models the probability of a specific number of rare events (k) occurring in a fixed interval (N), given an average rate (λ). This is ideal for safety failure rates.

#### A. Modeling Zero Failures (k=0)

If the system drives N real-world miles and observes **zero** critical failures (k=0), we use the upper bound calculation derived from the Poisson process to establish confidence.

1. **Formula (Upper Bound):** The one-sided confidence interval for the true failure rate (λ) given k=0 failures is:  
   λUB​=N−ln(1−C)​
   
   - C: Confidence level (e.g., 99% or C=0.99).
   - N: Total exposure (miles).
   - λUB​: The upper bound of the failure rate (the worst-case risk we can assure with C confidence).

2. **Example Calculation:**
   
   - Target Confidence C=0.99.
   - Total Validated Exposure N=1,000,000 miles (Real + Validated Sim).
   - λUB​=1,000,000−ln(1−0.99)​≈1,000,0004.605​=4.605×10−6 failures per mile.

3. **Safety Case Argument:** "Based on 1 million miles of zero observed failures, we are 99% confident that the true failure rate is no worse than 4.6 failures per million miles."

#### B. Modeling Few Failures (k>0)

If k failures are observed, the calculation uses the **Chi-Squared distribution** to find the confidence interval, which is the exact method for finding confidence intervals for Poisson means.

1. **Formula (Upper Bound for k>0):**  
   λUB​=2Nχ2(k+1),C2​​
   
   - χ2(k+1),C2​: The value from the Chi-Squared distribution with 2(k+1) degrees of freedom at the desired confidence level C.

2. **Example Calculation:**
   
   - Assume k=2 failures observed in N=1,000,000 miles.
   - Degrees of freedom =2(2+1)=6.
   - For C=0.99, the χ2 value is ≈16.81.
   - λUB​=2×1,000,00016.81​≈8.4×10−6 failures per mile.

### Step 4: Integrating Extreme Value Analysis (EVA)

While the Poisson method bounds the *rate* of events, EVA bounds the *severity* of the events that do occur.

1. **Process:** Use the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution to model the lowest tail of the TTC distribution (i.e., the most severe near-misses).
2. **Extrapolation:** Extrapolate the fitted GEV model to determine the **Return Level**—the expected minimum TTC value we would observe if we drove for 10 or 100 million miles.
3. **Safety Case Argument:** This allows you to state: "While our observed failure rate is bounded by λUB​, our EVA shows that the probability of a catastrophic TTC<0.5s event is lower than 10−9 per mile, demonstrating exceptional margin for the most severe risks."

### Step 5: Statistical Comparison to Baseline

The final step is crucial for proving improvement. Even if λUB​ is high, the system is deemed safer if it is significantly *lower* than the baseline system (λUBBaseline​).

1. **Paired Hypothesis Testing:** Use the **Difference in Proportions Test** (Z-test) to prove the reduction in the failure rate is statistically significant, as detailed previously (Example 1).
2. **Safety Case Argument:** "We reduced the required ASIL D trigger event rate from 5×10−5 failures/mile in SBaseline​ to 2×10−5 failures/mile in SNew​. This 60% reduction is statistically significant (p<0.001) and directly validates the effectiveness of the new checker stack."

# STPA

## Step 1: Define purpose of the analysis

STPA starts by identifying any **unacceptable losses**. Once unacceptable losses and the **system boundary** are determined, system-level hazards are identified.

## Step 2: Model the control structure

developing a system model referred to as a **control structure**. The control structure illustrates the functional interactions between the system components by representing the system as a series of feedback control loops. The control structure can be created at various levels of abstraction, depend-ing on the maturity of the system.

## Step 3: Identify Unsafe Control Actions (UCA)

UCAs are identified for every control action in the control structure. Each control action (CA) is analysed to identify how the CA would manifest into a UCA. To identify a UCA, the CA is usually considered together with a particular context and worst-case environment. There are several categories of UCAs:

• Not providing the CA leads to a hazard.

• Providing the CA incorrectly or when not needed leads to a hazard.

• Providing a CA too early or too late or in the wrong order leads to a hazard.

• Providing the CA too long or stopping the CA too soon leads to a hazard.

## Step 4: Identify loss scenarios

Possible loss scenarios, which describe the causal factors(CFs) that can lead to the UCAs, are identified by analysing the specific control loops of the control actions.

## Notes on STPA

- Numerous studies have confirmed that STPA is a powerful qualitative analysis tool, however, **it lacks quantitative assessment.** STPA needs to be supplemented with other approaches to adequately support the decision making on risk assessment. 

- The authors have also developed another novel approach which combines in- and out-degree centrality numbers with the entropy weights method, to prioritise the unsafe control actions identified in this case study. Firstly, the relationships among losses, hazards, UCAs, and causal factors were highlighted for each UCA, with an example illustrated in Fig. 4. In various fields of network applications, determining the importance of a node based on its connections is essential (Krnc and Škrekovski, 2020). In-degree centrality refers to the number of edges directed towards a node, while out-degree centrality refers to the edges that are outgoing from the node. Both these measures are used to highlight the centrality and significance of a node within a complex system (Csató, 2017). The approach prioritised UCAs by utilising two centrality measures: in-degree centrality, which is linked to the causal factors identified during analysis, and out-degree centrality, which corresponds to the associated hazards. To assign greater significance and enable an objective assessment of these centrality measures, the entropy weights method was applied (Karaca and Moonis, 2022). The entropy  weight method has previously been applied in diverse researchinvestigations and has proven effective, particularly in decision-making processes (Kumar et al., 2021). By integrating these methods, an objective and pertinent ranking of the UCAs was achieved.

- A significant property of STPA is its safety control structure.

When faced with conflicting priorities in an AV safety case study, particularly those involving trade-offs, a systems engineer must rely on a structured, objective process rooted in the ISO 26262 standard for functional safety. The most critical thing is assessed based on the potential for unmitigated harm.

In summary, the most critical thing is to prioritize the objective hazard with the highest ASIL ranking, followed by the one with the least fault tolerance.

> **For AVs, the focus is generally on preventing high-severity consequences even if they are rare.**

## 1. Establish the Safety Criterion: ASIL Rank

The most critical factor is determined by the Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) rank of the involved hazards. This rank provides an objective, quantitative measure of criticality.

ASIL Determination: ASIL is derived from a hazard's combination of three factors:

1. Severity (S): The extent of harm (e.g., Catastrophic, Severe, Moderate).

2. Exposure (E): The probability or frequency of the operating situation occurring.

3. Controllability (C): The ability of the driver/passenger/other agents to avoid the harm if the failure occurs.2
- Rule: The system requirement or component related to the highest ASIL rank (D $\rightarrow$ A) is always the most critical priority. ASIL D hazards (e.g., unmitigated loss of steering or braking) must be addressed before any lower ASIL-ranked issue.
  
  ![](data:image/png;base64,)
  
  ![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 2. Assess Conflict Through Fault Tolerance

If two conflicting priorities share the same ASIL rank (e.g., both are ASIL C), the conflict is resolved by assessing which priority offers the least fault tolerance or the greatest chance of a single-point failure.

Fault Tolerance Assessment: I would investigate the proposed solutions for both priorities:

- Priority A: Addresses an issue with $N=2$ redundant components.

- Priority B: Addresses an issue with $N=1$ primary component and no true redundancy (a single-point failure path).

- Decision: Priority B is more critical because it presents an immediate, higher probability of system failure if the single component fails, regardless of the equivalent ASIL rank. The goal is to eliminate single points of failure in high-ASIL systems first.

## 3. Utilize STOA to Quantify Operational Risk

If the conflict remains, the decision must be operationalized using the **Safety and Threat Operational Analysis** (STOA) data.

- Frequency vs. Severity Trade-off: Conflicts often arise between a High-Severity/Low-Frequency event and a Low-Severity/High-Frequency event.

- Example Conflict: (A) Fix a rare, catastrophic sensor-fusion failure (ASIL D, $10^{-8} \text{ /hr}$). VS. (B) Fix a common, minor jerk violation during a turn (ASIL B, $10^{-4} \text{ /hr}$).

- Decision: The priority that causes the system to violate its Quantitative Safety Goals (e.g., maximum allowable $\text{PFH}$) or the one with the highest Fatal Injury Risk Exposure based on real-world data is deemed more critical. For AVs, the focus is generally on preventing high-severity consequences even if they are rare.

In summary, **the most critical thing is not subjective preference, but the objective hazard with the highest ASIL ranking, followed by the one with the least fault tolerance.**

# 1. Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) ⚠️

HARA is a systematic process used to identify and evaluate potential hazards associated with a vehicle's operation, particularly for safety-critical systems like autonomous vehicles. It is often a key requirement for standards like ISO 26262. The goal is to determine unacceptable hazards and risks and then define safety goals to mitigate them.

#### HARA Methodology

The HARA process typically involves these steps:

- Item Definition: The first step is to define the item or system under analysis, outlining its purpose and functionality within the vehicle, including its operational modes.

- Hazard Identification: Brainstorming potential hazards, which are potential sources of harm. This can include hazards from system failures, environmental conditions, or human error.

- Risk Assessment: For each identified hazard, the risk is assessed based on three key factors:

- Severity (S): How bad are the consequences if the hazard occurs? This measures the potential impact.

- Exposure (E): How often is the vehicle exposed to the conditions that could lead to the hazard?.

- Controllability (C): How much can the driver or another system do to prevent the hazard from leading to an accident?.

- ASIL Classification: Based on the S, E, and C ratings, each hazard is assigned an Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL). ASIL ratings range from ASIL A (lowest safety requirement) to ASIL D (highest safety requirement) and are used to prioritize risks and define safety measures.

- Safety Goals and Requirements: Based on the ASIL ratings, the HARA process defines safety goals and high-level safety requirements to reduce the risk to an acceptable level through design changes and safety mechanisms.

---

# 2. Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) ⚙️

FMEA is a systematic, step-by-step approach to identify and prioritize potential failures in a design, manufacturing process, or system. It was first developed by the U.S. military in the 1940s and was later adopted by the automotive industry. The "failure mode" is the way something might fail, while "effects analysis" studies the consequences of those failures on the system.

#### FMEA Methodology

FMEA can be performed on a design (DFMEA) or a process (PFMEA). The methodology involves these steps:

- Team Building & Scoping: A multidisciplinary team is assembled to define the scope and boundaries of the analysis, which can be at the system, subsystem, or component level.

- Identify Functions & Failures: The team identifies the function of each part of the system. For each function, potential failure modes (e.g., "fails to brake") and their effects on the system and customer are brainstormed.

- Risk Assessment & Prioritization: Each potential failure mode is rated on three scales, typically from 1 to 10:

- Severity (S): The seriousness of the effect.

- Occurrence (O): The likelihood of the failure mode happening.

- Detection (D): The likelihood of the failure being detected before it reaches the end user.

- Risk Priority Number (RPN): A RPN is calculated by multiplying the three scores ($S \times O \times D$). Failures with a high RPN are prioritized for mitigation.

- Action Plans & Mitigation: The team develops action plans to reduce the RPN, such as redesigning components, enhancing controls, or improving detection methods. FMEA is an iterative process that should be updated as the design changes or new issues are discovered.

---

### 3. Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) 🧠

STPA is a modern, systems-based hazard analysis method that goes beyond traditional techniques, which often focus on component failures. It analyzes the entire system, including software, human operators, and their interactions, to identify hazards that can arise from complex system interactions and performance limitations.

# STPA Methodology

The STPA method provides a structured, four-step framework:

- Step 1: Define the System and its Purpose: The first step is to define the system boundaries, identify unacceptable "losses" (e.g., loss of life, injury, downtime), and define the hazards that can lead to those losses.

- Step 2: Model the Control Structure: The system is modeled as a hierarchy of control loops, showing how different components (controllers) and human operators command and receive feedback from the system. This helps to identify hazardous system interactions and missing requirements.

- Step 3: Identify Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs): For every control action in the model, the analyst systematically identifies ways it could be unsafe. This involves asking four key questions:

- Is the control action provided when it shouldn't be?

- Is the control action not provided when it should be?

- Is the control action provided too early, too late, for too long, or too short?

- Step 4: Identify Causal Scenarios: For each UCA, the team identifies the scenarios that could cause it. This involves analyzing the entire control loop to determine how a flawed process model, incorrect feedback, or a flawed algorithm could lead to the unsafe action. The goal is to identify all possible accident scenarios, regardless of their probability. The output of this analysis is a set of safety constraints and requirements to prevent these scenarios.

# AVSC - Metrics and Methods for Safety Assessment

**Criteria for DDT-Relevant System Level Metrics**

1. The metric has an established relationship to safety outcomes for human drivers.

2. Real-world ADS performance can be measured and assessed practicably by ADS developers and manufacturers.

3. The metrics and associated methods are technology neutral and can be consistently applied to different ADS usage specifications and across test venues

**Safety Goals**

The following high-level goals for desired societal impact were used to guide the development of this best practice:

**1.** **Reduce the number and severity of crashes.**

**2.** **Perform contextually safe vehicle motion control.**

Safety performance metrics provide quantitative evidence and help developers substantiate their safety goals. The recommended safety outcomes are direct measures of the safety goals.

![](/Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2025-12-14-19-38-42-image.png)

![](/Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2025-12-14-19-41-30-image.png)

As ADS-operated vehicles become more widespread, metrics indicative of competent DDT performance such as safety envelope maintenance; predictable vehicle motion control; and the time required to detect, recognize, and react to objects and events should be considered as causal factors for crashes. There are similar measurements used to assess traffic safety performance of human-driven vehicles, including time-to-collision, hard braking, and sudden steering maneuvers. **Because an SAE level 4 or 5 ADS performs the complete DDT instead of a human driver, it can be assumed that violations of a threshold for these types of metrics should be a valid indicator of safety performance.**

![](/Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2025-12-14-19-44-02-image.png)

### Safety envelope maintenance

A safety envelope is a kinematically defined state space around a vehicle that represents a buffer between the subject vehicle and other objects in the environment. Maintaining a safety envelope contributes to a safer driving environment by allowing the ADS time and space to respond to the actions of nearby road users and other objects and by allowing other road users to potentially correct erroneous driving. With time and space, an ADS-DV can execute maneuvers (e.g., braking or steering) that may reduce the likelihood of a crash or the potential severity of impact compared to no action being taken (i.e., serves as surrogate measure for potential severity).

## DDT Performance Metrics

The safety performance metrics in Table 3 can be used to assess ADS safety in a range of scenarios. One useful way to categorize scenarios is by assessing probability of scenario occurrence based on risk . Typical driving scenarios are encountered frequently and have relatively low risk. Critical driving scenarios, for example, re-establishing a safety buffer, occur less frequently and have relatively high risk.

![](/Users/xonxis/Library/Application%20Support/marktext/images/2025-12-14-19-56-14-image.png)

- ADS developers and manufacturers should establish practicable ADS safety performance thresholds for metrics specific to their ADS design, ODD, and usage specification.

- To advance the goals  thresholds for crash severity and frequency should be set such that they improve upon matched baseline aggregate human driver safety performance of the transportation system within the ODD where human performance data is available.

- Manufacturers should document their sampling strategy and describe how it accounts for significant exposure of DDT performance events and ODD characteristics

- Finally, the sample size for the segmented population’s risk exposure, n, should be reported in all cases and should be representative of the risk associated with the ADS usage specification, including foreseeable interactions with other road users.

### Normalization

Normalizing results refers to adjusting data with different measurement scales and risk levels to enable comparison across data sets and correct for known limitations. For example, two safety envelope violations per 100,000 pedestrian encounters or four citable offenses per 10,000 intersection traversals. Metrics in this document are framed in terms of the count or duration of occurrences of safety relevant events. When determining event frequency, measurements should be normalized by risk exposure to adjust data with different scales [73] [74]. Exposure normalization improves the comparability of results across different data sets by creating a common scale and improves interpretability and portability of results. For example, the overall number of crashes does not enable an assessment of safety unless the exposure is also known (e.g., number of pedestrian interactions). Mathematically, normalization can be approached in many ways. The appropriate approach depends on the sample size and nature of the data. In the near-term with small sample sizes, descriptive statistics (i.e., mean, median, mode, range, and quartile deviation) can be used. Larger data sets may be normalized (e.g., Z score values) based on distribution of the occurrence and providing an indication of exposure to the event (e.g., Poisson, binomial, negative binomial distributions). One approach to normalize measurements and obtain the mean rate of occurrence, f, is to divide by the sample size (i.e., the risk exposure factor), n:

$f = measurement/n$

Sampling strategies should determine an appropriate time horizon that is resilient to temporary changes in performance. Larger data sets yield more significant and stable results. At the same time, crash risk is known to vary over time for humans (e.g., based on experience [69] [75]) and similarly, ADS performance is anticipated to improve over time (i.e., as machine learning algorithms improve with richer data sets and as AVs become a larger proportion of the on-road vehicle fleet). The time horizon for the sampling strategy should consider these factors.

**To normalize data for risk exposure, this best practice recommends segmenting crash data by the type of service offered:**

• If the service is passenger transport, then taxi crash rates can be relevant.

• If the service is goods delivery, then package delivery service crash rates can be relevant.

• If the service is long-haul trucking, then crash rates on city roads may be excluded from the analysis (in 2017,the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) determined that there were 3,212 billion VMT, 70% of which was

in urban geography [77]).

### Considerations for Statistical Confidence and Trends

Statistical confidence is what allows conclusions to be drawn or inferred based on the evidence collected. Statistical confidence quantitatively describes the ­ uncertainty

associated with the likelihood of encountering an event again over a certain measurement period (such as time, VMT, exposure, etc.).

Confidence that crash metrics are representative of aggregate system performance can be calculated in several ways. One such method is outlined in the RAND methodology [78]. Confidence in the stability of ADS safety performance vis-à-vis a metric may be assessed using a moving average that measures performance over time. There are several ways to calculate a moving average. One example calculation for parameter, p, is provided below for the moving average of acceleration, p:

$p^-_i = 1/n \sum^n_{i=1}{p_i}$

where n specifies the sample size (e.g., the time horizon), which is defined by an ADS developer or manufacturer,i is a measurement point between 1 and n; and pi is acceleration at point i. The gradient is assessed as the difference between a moving average at the current time and a historical moving average over the time, and compared to a treshold $\triangle p^-_{ref} $: 

${p_2 - p_1}/{t_2-t_1} > \triangle p^-_{ref}$

Transportation and many metrics related to transportation safety are influenced by national and regional trends. Factors such as vehicle ownership, land use, economic fluctuations, and an aging population may be reflected in national crash data metrics [79]. Trends associated with factors such as these need to be monitored because they can influence baselines that may be used for comparison to ADS safety performance.

# AVCS thresholds

The initial step for an ADS

developer is to establish a null hypothesis for targeted data collection and analysis. For instance, the null hypothesis

for the selected scenario in which a pedestrian is walking within the lane of travel of the ADS-DV could be, “The

lateral distance does not increase between the SV and pedestrian from the time of initial detection to the time of

passing.” Based on this initial hypothesis, an ADS manufacturer can opt to procure NDS scenarios from a third

party, collect the data themselves, or filter data relevant to the scenario from a larger dataset. Regardless of the

source of data, the analysis process should include the following steps, as illustrated in FIGURE 3.

• **Step** **5.3.1**: Performing an exploratory data analysis to ensure that the data needed to test a hypothesis is available and applicable, as well as relevant to the ODD of interest. The scope of this data should be consistent with the scenario definition and ODD context from 5.1; otherwise, the data collection will need to be augmented to fill any gaps.

• **Step** **5.3.2**: Execute the appropriate statistical hypothesis testing.

• **Step** **5.3.3**: Statistical analysis.

▪ **Step** **5.3.3.1**: Sample size requirements and statistical power analysis.

▪ **Step** **5.3.3.2**: Understanding uncertainties, error propagation, and accuracy.

• **Step** **5.3.4**: Utilize reference values for ADS performance thresholds.

#### Sample Size Requirements and Statistical Power Analysis

Determining the right sample size is a function of acceptable error, standard deviation, and confidence interval

(z score). The uncertainty in estimating a safety metric when actual values are not available (as with lateral

distance in the example scenario) depends on the intrinsic variability of the measurements as well as the number

of observations available. The impact of errors in estimating any variable can typically be reduced by increasing the

sample size. ADS developers can decide on an appropriate sample size based on acceptable error (or risk tolerance

of an ADS developer). For example:

• For standard deviation (SD) = 0.5 m, error = 0.05 m, z = 1.96, then sample size could be 385.

• For SD = 0.5 m, error = 0.1 m, z = 1.96, then sample size could be 96.

Statistical power analysis18 is another effective method to determine a minimum sample size for analysis [13] [14].

With a given statistical power (commonly accepted lower threshold of 80% or higher), the significance level

(commonly accepted lower threshold of 5%) and expected effect size (calculated to be 0.4 m based on differences

of mean and SD), the sample size required for a statistically significant analysis could be approximately 15019 (see

APPENDIX C).

# Study Guide: Lead Data Science Statistician

This role sits at the intersection of **Rigorous Statistics** and **Physical Engineering**. They do not want a "black box" AI approach; they want explainable, mathematically sound proofs of safety.

---

### **Topic 1: Causal Inference in Observational Data**

**The Problem:** You cannot run an A/B test that risks safety (e.g., "Let's turn off the LIDAR for 50% of cars"). You must use historical, observational data to prove that a specific software change *caused* an improvement in safety, rather than just random chance or easier driving conditions.

**Key Methods:**

- **Instrumental Variables (IV):** Used to isolate the "causal" effect when there is a hidden confounder.
  
  - *Example:* You want to know if **Software V2** reduces braking harshness. But V2 was only deployed in Phoenix (flat, dry), while V1 was in San Francisco (hilly). Geography is a confounder.
  
  - *The Instrument:* Find a variable correlated with the software assignment but *not* the braking outcome directly (e.g., "release rollout schedule").

- **Propensity Score Matching (PSM):** Re-weight your data so the "treatment" group (new software) and "control" group (old software) have statistically identical distributions of covariates (weather, speed, traffic density).

**Q: "How would you use Instrumental Variables to determine if a disengagement was caused by the software?"**

> **A:** "I would look for an instrument—a variable that affects the *condition* but not the *outcome* directly. For example, if we want to know if 'high sensor noise' causes disengagements, we can't just correlate them because difficult scenes cause both.
> 
> I would use **'Sun Glare Angle'** as an instrument. The sun angle is random and exogenous; it *causes* high sensor noise (camera washout), but it doesn't inherently make a driver pull over unless the *sensor* fails. By regressing Disengagement on the 'prediction' of noise caused by the sun, we isolate the causal link between sensor failure and disengagement, removing the driver's behavior from the equation."
> 
> **The Scenario**
> 
> You want to know: **Does high Sensor Noise *cause* the human driver to panic and take control (Disengagement)?**
> 
> ** The Problem: The "Dirty" Data**
> 
> You can't just look at a graph of `Noise` vs. `Disengagements`.
> 
> - **Why?** Because a difficult driving scenario (like a busy, chaotic intersection) causes **both**:
>   
>   1. High sensor noise (lots of confusing data).
>   
>   2. Nervous drivers (who might take over just to be safe).
> 
> - **The Trap:** If you just look at the raw data, you might blame the sensor for the disengagement, when actually the driver just took over because the traffic was scary. The driver's behavior is "polluting" your data.
> 
> **The Solution: The "Clean" Prediction (Instrumental Variable)**
> 
> We use the **Sun Angle** as a "truth serum" because the sun is totally independent of the traffic or the driver's mood.
> 
> **Step 1: Create the "Predicted Noise" (The Filter)** Instead of using the *actual* sensor noise (which is polluted by the chaotic intersection), you build a mini-model that predicts how much noise *should* be there based **ONLY** on the sun's position.
> 
> - *Input:* Sun is low on the horizon (glare).
> 
> - *Output:* "Predicted Noise" is High.
> 
> - *Crucial Detail:* This "Predicted Noise" has nothing to do with traffic or the driver. It is a "clean" variable created purely by physics.
> 
> **Step 2: The Final Test (The Regression)** Now, you check the correlation between **Disengagement** and **Predicted Noise**.
> 
> - Since "Predicted Noise" is based *only* on the sun, it contains **zero** information about the driver's nervousness or the road complexity.
> 
> - Therefore, if you find a link here, you have proven that the **physics of the glare** caused the sensor to fail, which caused the disengagement. You have successfully "removed the driver from the equation."

---

### **Topic 2: Rare Event Modeling (The "Zero Crashes" Problem)**

**The Problem:** Crashes are extremely rare (1 in 100 million miles). If you train a standard model, it will predict "No Crash" 100% of the time and achieve 99.99% accuracy but fail the safety case.

**Key Methods:**

- **Extreme Value Theory (EVT):** specifically **Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT)**. Instead of modeling the *average* driving, you model the *tail* of the distribution (e.g., the top 0.1% of hardest braking events). You fit these to a **Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD)** to extrapolate the probability of an event you haven't seen yet (a crash).

- **Importance Sampling:** In simulation, you "tilt" the probability to make rare events (icy roads, jaywalkers) happen more often, then mathematically re-weight the results to calculate the real-world risk.

**Q: "We have petabytes of driving data, but almost zero crashes. How do you validate safety?"**

> **A:** "We cannot rely on simple counting statistics. I would apply **Extreme Value Theory (EVT)** using the **Peaks-Over-Threshold** method.
> 
> I would select a proxy metric, like 'Time-To-Collision' (TTC). We likely have thousands of 'near-miss' events where TTC dropped below 2 seconds. By fitting these tail events to a **Generalized Pareto Distribution**, I can mathematically extrapolate the probability of the TTC dropping to 0 (a crash), even if we have zero examples of it in the dataset. This allows us to quantify the risk of '1 in a billion' events using only '1 in a million' data."
> 
> How do you calculate the probability of a crash if your car has never crashed?
> 
> If you use standard statistics (like a Normal/Bell Curve), you will dangerously underestimate risk. Here is the practical breakdown of Extreme Value Theory (EVT) using the Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) method.
> 
> ### 1. The Core Concept: "Fat Tails"
> 
> In a standard Normal Distribution, events far from the average become impossible very quickly.
> 
> - **The Lie of the Bell Curve:** If driving risk followed a Bell Curve, a "5-sigma" event (a crash) would happen once every million years.
> 
> - **The Reality:** In the real world, "extreme" events happen much more often (financial crashes, earthquakes, car accidents). This is called a **"Heavy Tail"** or **"Fat Tail."**
> 
> EVT ignores the "average" (the center of the bell curve) and **only models the tail**.
> 
> ### 2. The Step-by-Step Methodology (POT)
> 
> Imagine you are analyzing **Braking Force (g)**. Most braking is gentle (0.1g - 0.3g). A crash is effectively an infinite deceleration, or let's say > 2.0g.
> 
> Step 1: Pick a Proxy Metric
> 
> You can't measure "crashes" because you don't have any. You need a continuous metric where "higher" means "closer to a crash."
> 
> - *Examples:* Deceleration (g-force), Inverse Time-to-Collision (iTTC).
> 
> Step 2: Set the Threshold ($u$)
> 
> This is the "Threshold" in Peaks-Over-Threshold. You draw a line in the sand, say at 0.6g (hard braking).
> 
> - You discard *all* data below 0.6g. It is irrelevant "safe" driving.
> 
> - You keep only the "Peaks" that go "Over the Threshold." These are your "near-misses."
> 
> Step 3: Calculate the "Excess"
> 
> For every event above 0.6g, you measure how much it exceeded the threshold.
> 
> - *Event A:* 0.65g (Excess = 0.05)
> 
> - *Event B:* 0.80g (Excess = 0.20)
> 
> **Step 4: Fit the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD)**
> 
> This is the statistical magic. Mathematics (specifically the Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem) tells us that no matter what the original distribution of driving data is, the excesses over a high enough threshold will always follow a Generalized Pareto Distribution.
> 
> The GPD formula looks roughly like this:
> 
> $G(x) = 1 - (1 + \xi \frac{x}{\sigma})^{-1/\xi}$
> 
> - **$\xi$ (Shape Parameter):** This implies how "fat" the tail is. A positive $\xi$ means the danger does not drop off quickly—risk remains high even at extreme values.
> 
> Step 5: Extrapolate to the Unseen
> 
> You have fitted the curve to your data (0.6g to 0.9g). Because you know the shape of the tail (GPD), you can mathematically extend that line out to 2.0g.
> 
> - Even though you have **zero** data points at 2.0g, the formula gives you a probability density for that value.
> 
> - **Result:** You can now say, "Based on our near-misses, the probability of a 2.0g crash event is 1 in 100 million miles," rather than just saying "We don't know."

---

### **Topic 3: Integrating Physics Constraints**

**The Problem:** A pure ML model might predict a car moved sideways by 10 meters in 0.1 seconds because of a sensor glitch. A statistician knows this is physically impossible.

**Key Methods:**

- **Kalman Filters (EKF/UKF):** The gold standard for state estimation. It combines a "Physics Prediction" (motion model) with a "Measurement" (sensor data) and weights them by their uncertainty.

- **Bayesian Priors:** Hard-coding physical laws as priors. If the probability of $Velocity > 200mph$ is non-zero, the model is wrong.

**Q: "How do you ensure your statistical models respect the laws of physics?"**

> **A:** "I believe in using **Physics-Informed Priors**. For example, when estimating the trajectory of a pedestrian, I wouldn't just use a regression line. I would use a **Kalman Filter** where the state transition matrix is defined by kinematic equations.
> 
> If the sensor data suggests a movement that violates the maximum possible acceleration of a human (e.g., 3g's), the Kalman Gain will naturally down-weight that measurement as 'noise' rather than 'signal.' This ensures our uncertainty bounds are realistic to the physical world, not just the data artifacts."

---

### **Topic 4: Behavioral & Leadership (The "Lead" Aspect)**

The Core Value: "Win with Integrity." Safety > Speed.

The Strategy: You must show you can stand up to a Product Manager who wants to launch.

**Q: "Tell me about a time you had to explain a complex statistical risk to a non-technical leader."**

> **A:** "In a previous project, we had a model with 95% accuracy, and leadership wanted to launch. However, I identified that the 5% error was clustered in 'heavy rain' scenarios—a bias in our training data.
> 
> I didn't talk about 'heteroscedasticity' or 'p-values.' I showed them a **Safety Case** visualization: 'In sunny weather, we are safer than a human. In rain, we are 10x riskier.' I framed it as an **Operational Design Domain (ODD)** limitation. I recommended we launch, but *hard-code* the system to disengage in rain. This allowed us to ship value immediately while maintaining 100% safety integrity."
